results.name: far_outside_range_yes_rate
results.description: Yes-rate for targets more than 20 below the smallest or above the largest example; observed above null means the model generalizes too narrowly beyond the example range (under-produces distant yeses), below means too broadly.
results.code:
# name: far_outside_range_yes_rate
# description: Yes-rate for targets more than 20 below the smallest or above the largest example; observed above null means the model generalizes too narrowly beyond the example range (under-produces distant yeses), below means too broadly.
def test_statistic(df):
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    uniq = sets.unique()
    parsed = {s: np.array([int(x) for x in s.split(",")]) for s in uniq}
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    lo = sets.map({s: a.min() for s, a in parsed.items()}).to_numpy()
    hi = sets.map({s: a.max() for s, a in parsed.items()}).to_numpy()
    sel = (t < lo - 20) | (t > hi + 20)
    return float(r[sel].mean()) if sel.any() else 0.0

results.name: sequential_yes_dependence
results.description: P(yes | previous trial yes) minus P(yes | previous trial no) over consecutive trials (trial_index step of 1); observed above null means response perseveration / carry-over that the trial-independent model does not produce.

results.name: within_range_gap_yes_rate
results.description: Yes-rate for non-example targets strictly between the smallest and largest example of multi-example sets; observed above null means people fill in the example range (interval-like) more than the model predicts, below means less.
results.code:
# name: within_range_gap_yes_rate
# description: Yes-rate for non-example targets strictly between the smallest and largest example of multi-example sets; observed above null means people fill in the example range (interval-like) more than the model predicts, below means less.
def test_statistic(df):
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    uniq = sets.unique()
    parsed = {s: np.array([int(x) for x in s.split(",")]) for s in uniq}
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    lo = sets.map({s: a.min() for s, a in parsed.items()}).to_numpy()
    hi = sets.map({s: a.max() for s, a in parsed.items()}).to_numpy()
    n = sets.map({s: len(a) for s, a in parsed.items()}).to_numpy()
    isex = np.zeros(len(df), bool)
    for s, a in parsed.items():
        m = (sets == s).to_numpy()
        isex[m] = np.isin(t[m], a)
    sel = (n >= 2) & (t > lo) & (t < hi) & ~isex
    return float(r[sel].mean()) if sel.any() else 0.0

results.name: four_vs_two_example_yes_gap
results.description: Yes-rate on 4-example sets minus yes-rate on 2-example sets; observed more negative than null means people tighten generalization with more examples more than the model does, more positive means less.

results.name: trial_index_slope
results.description: Correlation between trial_index and yes response; nonzero observed vs a ~0 null means the yes-rate drifts over the session (fatigue/learning), which the stationary model cannot produce (sign gives drift direction).

results.name: near_miss_yes_rate
results.description: Yes-rate for targets 1-3 away from the nearest example (and not an example itself); observed above null means people generalize by numerical proximity more than the rule/interval posterior predicts.
results.code:
# name: near_miss_yes_rate
# description: Yes-rate for targets 1-3 away from the nearest example (and not an example itself); observed above null means people generalize by numerical proximity more than the rule/interval posterior predicts.
def test_statistic(df):
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    uniq = sets.unique()
    parsed = {s: np.array([int(x) for x in s.split(",")]) for s in uniq}
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    out = np.full(len(df), np.inf)
    for s, a in parsed.items():
        m = (sets == s).to_numpy()
        out[m] = np.abs(t[m][:, None] - a[None, :]).min(axis=1)
    sel = (out >= 1) & (out <= 3)
    return float(r[sel].mean()) if sel.any() else 0.0

results.name: between_set_yes_rate_sd
results.description: Standard deviation across example sets (with >=10 trials) of each set's yes-rate; observed above null means generalization breadth varies more from set to set than the model predicts (model too homogeneous), below means less.
results.code:
# name: between_set_yes_rate_sd
# description: Standard deviation across example sets (with >=10 trials) of each set's yes-rate; observed above null means generalization breadth varies more from set to set than the model predicts (model too homogeneous), below means less.
def test_statistic(df):
    g = df.groupby(df["number_set"].astype(str))["rating"].agg(["mean", "size"])
    g = g[g["size"] >= 10]
    return float(g["mean"].std()) if len(g) > 1 else 0.0

results.name: singleton_set_yes_rate
results.description: Yes-rate on trials whose set has a single example; observed above null means the model generalizes too narrowly from one example (too strong a size principle / rule preference), below means too broadly.
results.code:
# name: singleton_set_yes_rate
# description: Yes-rate on trials whose set has a single example; observed above null means the model generalizes too narrowly from one example (too strong a size principle / rule preference), below means too broadly.
def test_statistic(df):
    n = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.count(",").to_numpy() + 1
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    sel = n == 1
    return float(r[sel].mean()) if sel.any() else 0.0
